items.title: The Governance of AI in Education: Developing Ethical Policy Frameworks for Adaptive Learning Technologies
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has transformed adaptive learning by personalizing instruction, automating assessments, and enhancing student engagement. However, the ethical challenges of AI governance, including algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, transparency gaps, and accountability issues, necessitate a structured regulatory framework. This study develops the Ethical AI Governance Framework for Adaptive Learning (EAGFAL) to address governance gaps and ensure fair, transparent, and responsible AI adoption in education. Using secondary data analysis and comparative case studies, the study examines global AI governance models, regulatory best practices, and ethical risks in AIdriven education. Findings highlight that inconsistent regulatory approaches contribute to disparities in AI deployment, with some regions favoring market-driven AI policies, while others enforce strict legal oversight. The study recommends bias mitigation strategies, explainable AI mechanisms, and robust data governance policies to ensure AI-driven education remains inclusive, ethical, and student-centered. EAGFAL offers practical policy insights for governments, educators, and AI developers, advocating for cross-sector collaboration to align AI innovation with ethical responsibility. Future research should explore long-term impacts, scalability, and evolving governance structures for ethical AI integration in education.

items.title: The impact of AI chatbot service quality on consumer purchase intention: the cognitive and affective mediating mechanisms
items.abstract: Introduction The increasing prevalence of artificial intelligence chatbots in e-commerce raises questions about how the service quality dimensions of AI chatbots may influence consumer purchase intentions. Drawing on Expectation-Confirmation Theory, the Information Systems Success Model, and the Technology Acceptance Model, this study proposes a conceptual framework to examine these relationships. Methods Survey data were collected from 493 Chinese consumers with prior experience using AI chatbots. The study examined perceived personalization, social presence, information quality, and human-AI service continuity as possible antecedents of purchase intention. Perceived usefulness and satisfaction were treated as mediating variables. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used for the analysis with 5,000 bootstrapped resamples. Results Perceived personalization, social presence, information quality, and human-AI service continuity were associated with perceived usefulness. Additionally, perceived personalization, information quality, and human-AI service continuity were positively associated with satisfaction. Conversely, social presence did not show a significant direct effect on satisfaction. Both perceived usefulness and satisfaction are linked to purchase intention, with satisfaction having a stronger direct connection. The mediation analysis revealed that perceived usefulness and satisfaction mediate the relationship between AI chatbot service quality and purchase intention. The only exception was the indirect effect of social presence through satisfaction, which was not statistically significant. Discussion This study seeks to contribute to understanding how the service quality of AI chatbots influences consumers’ purchase intentions through perceived usefulness and satisfaction. The results indicate that information quality is the most significant among the service quality dimensions in AI-mediated interactions. The lack of a significant direct impact of social presence on satisfaction suggests that, in utilitarian-oriented e-commerce environments, consumers are more likely to prioritize functional service features over social–emotional factors when assessing AI chatbot services. These findings may inform e-commerce practitioners seeking to improve AI-driven customer service by emphasizing information accuracy and completeness, enhancing personalization, and fostering seamless human-AI service continuity to drive purchase conversions.

items.title: The impact of AI on the advertising industry in Spain: uncertainty and threats according to professionals in the sector
items.abstract: This exploratory study aims to analyse the perceptions of professionals in the field of marketing and advertising regarding the risks and threats associated with the growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the sector. Through a survey with a sample of 373 marketing, advertising, and branded content professionals in Spain, the concerns of participants were uncovered regarding the quality of AI-generated content, the potential loss of creativity and originality, the impact on job security, and the need for human oversight. While the participants appreciate the operational utility of AI, they also warn of its ethical, expressive, and strategic limitations. The findings reveal a perspective that is critical, although not technophobic, which calls for regulatory frameworks, specialised training, and responsible use. In regards to the practical implications, this study highlights the tension that accompanies automation in the creative field and underscores the importance of ethical, balanced, and human-focused use of such technology, which is the prerequisite for a responsible transition toward the use of AI in the advertising industry. Given the context, it is imperative to understand how the transformation of the industry due to the introduction of these technologies is interpreted by the professionals who experience them firsthand. This study is one of the first to evaluate the level of acceptance of AI tools among professionals in the advertising industry in Spain.

items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become a game changer in the healthcare industry, with profound effects on operational effectiveness and service quality. This empirical study examines how AI adoption affects the provision of healthcare services, concentrating on two main aspects: improving operational efficiency (resource allocation, patient waiting times, administrative workflows, and cost reduction) and improving service quality (diagnostic accuracy, patient satisfaction, and care personalization). The study used a standardized survey instrument that was given to [N] administrators and healthcare workers from various healthcare facilities, utilizing a quantitative research approach. To find statistically significant correlations between AI adoption levels and key performance measures, data were analyzed using multiple regression, correlation analysis, and descriptive statistics.

items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Technology Applications on the Employment Structure of the Labor Force
items.abstract: Advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) have occurred alongside digitization, big data, and computing power and have significantly impacted how the global labor market works. This paper examines the effects of AI applications on the labor market and the structure of the workforce. The main method of research is literature review; academic articles on the implementation of AI and its effects on the workforce are reviewed and analyzed to understand skill-biased and task-biased technological changes along with displacement, reinforcement, and productivity effects of AI. This paper finds that AI contributes to increasing the demand for highly skilled workers who would be able to complement intelligent systems while reducing the demand for simple professions and jobs that can be automated. However, the overall impact on employment is weak so far due to the offset of job losses resulting from automation by the emergence of new job positions at more productive companies using AI.

items.title: The Implementation of STEM Approach on English Learning in Students Writing Activities at SMP Negeri 12 Gorontalo
items.abstract: The integration of Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics (STEM) into English language instruction has emerged as an innovative approach to support meaningful learning experiences and enhance students’ writing development. This study aimed to explore the implementation of STEM-based English writing instruction and examine its contribution to students’ engagement and writing development at SMP Negeri 12 Gorontalo. Employing a descriptive qualitative design, the study involved one English teacher and twenty-six eighth-grade students. Data were collected through classroom observations, semi-structured interviews, and documentation of students’ written products. The findings revealed that STEM was implemented through a series of interconnected learning activities, including direct observation, technology-assisted learning, collaborative project construction, descriptive writing tasks, revision activities, and reflective presentations. The integration of STEM elements facilitated students’ active participation throughout the learning process and promoted behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement. Furthermore, STEM-based activities supported students’ writing development by providing authentic learning experiences that enabled them to generate ideas, organize information, expand vocabulary use, and produce contextualized descriptive texts. The findings also indicated that project-based STEM activities fostered creativity, collaboration, and problem-solving skills, which contributed positively to the quality of students’ written products. Although some students continued to experience difficulties related to grammar and language accuracy, most were able to communicate ideas effectively and produce writing that reflected their observation and project experiences. These findings suggest that STEM-based English writing instruction offers a meaningful pedagogical framework for enhancing student engagement and supporting writing development through contextual, collaborative, and project-oriented learning experiences.

items.title: The Mediating Roles of Satisfaction and Perceived Intelligence In Chatgpt Adoption Among Research and Development Employees: An Extended Technology Acceptance Model
items.abstract: This study examines how employees in corporate research and development (R&D) units form the intention to use ChatGPT at work, a population that remains underexplored compared with the student samples dominating prior research. Building on an extended Technology Acceptance Model, the study tests whether perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and awareness shape behavioural intention to use, with satisfaction and perceived intelligence positioned as dual mediators. Data from 190 R&D employees in Tangerang Regency, Indonesia, obtained through purposive sampling, were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). All eight hypothesised direct paths were supported: ease of use and usefulness strengthen satisfaction, awareness builds perceived intelligence, and all five predictors raise behavioural intention, with perceived usefulness as the dominant driver. Perceived intelligence and satisfaction partially transmit the effects of awareness and usefulness, respectively. The findings direct organisations to anchor workplace artificial intelligence adoption strategies in demonstrated usefulness and structured awareness-building.

items.title: The Multidimensional Relationship Between Algorithmic Media Content Awareness and Artificial Intelligence Literacy: A Study on University Students
items.abstract: This study aims to examine the relationship between university students’ algorithmic content awareness and artificial intelligence literacy levels, and to reveal the interaction pattern between these two competency domains. As algorithmic systems increasingly shape how individuals access information, users’ ability to understand and critically evaluate these systems has become essential. In this context, the study highlights the role of cognitive awareness beyond mere technological exposure. The study was conducted using a correlational survey design, a quantitative research method. Data were collected from 534 students enrolled at Selçuk University through a structured questionnaire. The dataset was filtered based on missing data, straight-lining responses (longstring bias), and inconsistent response patterns in reverse-coded items. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), mediation analysis, and canonical correlation analysis were employed in the data analysis process. The findings indicate a positive and moderate significant relationship between algorithmic awareness and artificial intelligence literacy (r = .464, p < .001). Structural model results show that algorithmic awareness significantly predicts artificial intelligence literacy (β = .47, p < .001). Canonical correlation analysis revealed a moderate level of shared variance between the two variable sets (Rc = .473; Rc² = .224). However, social media usage time did not have a significant indirect effect on artificial intelligence literacy through algorithmic awareness (ab = .025, p = .244). The results suggest that technological exposure alone is not sufficient; rather, artificial intelligence literacy develops through cognitive processes associated with critical awareness of algorithmic systems.

items.title: The Psychological Mechanisms and Social Implications of Over-Trust in AI Chat-Based on GPT-4 Persuasion Experiments
items.abstract: As large language models have been increasingly applied to daily life in information seeking and decision-making, public trust in AI output has greatly improved. This brings about the worry that human critical thinking could become impaired. Using Salvi et al.'s GPT-4 conversational persuasion experiment as a start, this paper adopts a literature review method and relies on the theory of automation bias as well as cognitive laziness. This paper uses literature review as the way of research and utilizes the theories such as automation bias and cognitive laziness, etc., to explore the psychological mechanism behind the power of AI's ability to persuade others, and how it affects different people's minds. Findings indicate that the notable persuasiveness of AI stems primarily from two interrelated psychological mechanisms: cognitive laziness, which inclines individuals to forgo independent verification, and algorithm worship, which inclines individuals to delegate cognitive authority to AI systems. Both mechanisms manifest across adolescent and adult populations and may contribute to the erosion of critical thinking through prolonged AI use. The national, corporate, educational, individual levels response strategies are put forward in this paper, and the future research directions including cross-cultural comparison studies, longitudinal follow-up researches and individual-difference study plans are given out.

items.title: The Relationship Between Artificial Intelligence Literacy and Artificial Intelligence Anxiety: The Case of Medical School Resident Physicians
items.abstract: Aim: To examine the relationship between resident physicians' Artificial Intelligence literacy levels and their anxiety towards Artificial Intelligence, and to evaluate differences according to sociodemographic variables. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 296 resident physicians working at Necmettin Erbakan University Faculty of Medicine between January and February 2025. Data were collected via an online survey comprising a sociodemographic information form and questions regarding attitudes, experiences of AI, the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, and the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale. The data were analysed using the SPSS 25.0 programme, with independent simple t-tests, one-way ANOVA, and Pearson's correlation analysis being employed. The significance level was set at p<0.05. Results: Scale scores were found to be significantly higher among those who spent more time online, those with experience with AI, and individuals interested in Artificial Intelligence. The Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale score was higher in women and in individuals who believed that artificial intelligence could replace them in the future. A significant negative correlation was found between the total Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale score and the usage and evaluation sub-dimension and the learning sub-dimension of the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale. Conclusion: This suggests that personal experiences and educational factors influence perceptions of artificial intelligence. Integrating Artificial Intelligence knowledge and applications into medical education may enhance physicians’ awareness and attitudes.

items.title: The relationship between self-determination theory–based L2 motivation and L2 achievement: A multilevel meta-analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Over the past decades, self-determination theory (SDT) has been widely applied in second language (L2) motivation research. The present study employed a multilevel meta-analysis to examine the direction and magnitude of the relationship between SDT-based L2 motivation and L2 achievement. We systematically searched ten English databases and pooled the data using random-effects models. A total of 74 eligible studies involving 220 estimates were included in the analyses. The results showed that both intrinsic motivation ( r = .318, p < .001) and extrinsic motivation ( r = .166, p < .001) were significantly and positively correlated with L2 achievement. Two autonomous dimensions of extrinsic motivation—integrated regulation ( r =. 248, p < .001) and identified regulation ( r = .190, p < .001)—were positively related with L2 achievement, whereas controlled dimensions—introjected regulation ( r = .006, p = .866) and external regulation ( r = .010, p = .781)—were not. The aggregated associations between intrinsic/extrinsic motivation and L2 achievement were moderated by learning context and teaching mode. Theoretical and practical implications of this study are discussed.

items.title: The Role of Adaptive Learning Technologies in Personalized Education
items.abstract: As educational systems strive to move beyond "one-size-fits-all" pedagogical models, Adaptive Learning Technologies (ALTs) powered by Artificial Intelligence (AI) have emerged as a critical solution for personalization. This paper presents a systematic literature review examining the efficacy of ALTs in enhancing learner engagement, academic performance, and equity. Analyzing peer-reviewed studies published between 2019 and 2025, the review focuses on the transition from rule-based systems to advanced Machine Learning (ML) algorithms, specifically contrasting Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) with Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT) and Transformer-based models. Key findings indicate that ALTs yield a significant positive effect on cognitive learning outcomes and bolster student motivation (Chaudhry et al., 2025; Martinez & Anderson, 2024). However, the study identifies critical barriers, including the "cold start" problem, algorithmic bias in minority representations, and the "Black Box" opacity of neural networks (Baker & Hawn, 2021; Heaven, 2024). The paper concludes that while ALTs are potent tools for democratization, their sustainable success is contingent upon the integration of Explainable AI (XAI) frameworks and robust fairness-aware algorithms (Liu et al., 2024).

items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation in Smart and Sustainable Infrastructure Systems
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digitalization are rapidly transforming the planning, operation, maintenance and management of critical infrastructure. Planning, operation, maintenance and management of critical infrastructure is changing with Artificial Intelligence (AI) and digitalization. The review covers energy, transportation, water, building, and urban infrastructure sectors, focusing on predictive maintenance and forecasting, anomaly detection, adaptive control, digital twins, asset management, and resilience planning, highlighting the potential and limitations of AI and machine learning (ML) applications in these fields. AI's forecasting capabilities help with load balancing in electricity systems and the integration of renewable energy, while intelligent transportation systems enhance traffic management, safety, and infrastructure condition monitoring. AI is being used in water systems for leak detection, water quality monitoring, and drought forecasting, while in building applications, it's used for energy optimization, predictive control, and equipment fault detection. The review also explores cross cutting data quality, sensor reliability, interoperability, cybersecurity, human oversight, governance, ethics and regulatory compliance requirements. Although significant technology advancement has been realized, implementation is limited by existing legacy infrastructure, disparate data systems, limited technical capacity, funding and procurement barriers, cybersecurity, and demos from research and into large scale operating deployment. Special emphasis is placed on the concept of explainable AI, human in the loop decision making, risk based asset prioritization and ongoing model validation as ways to provide public accountability and reliability. Future directions are: climate adaptive infrastructure management, digital twins, edge computing, advanced remote sensing, continual and federated learning, dynamic network modeling, and hybrid human AI decision systems.

items.title: The role of digitalization in transforming training practices and employee learning perceptions: case study of an Algerian mobile network operator
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to understand the role of digitalization in transforming human resources (HR) training practices and employee learning perceptions. Design/methodology/approach As part of a qualitative study, we conducted 32 semi-structured interviews, which were transcribed and analyzed thematically using a manual approach. Findings The results reveal that digitalization reshapes training practices through strategic objectives while influencing learner experiences and engagement. However, its implementation is shaped by learner motivations, obstacles and organizational challenges. Research limitations/implications This study focuses only on the telecommunications industry and is limited to the Algerian context. Future research should adapt it to different sectors and countries. Originality/value By combining HR and employee perceptions in the under-researched Algerian telecommunications sector, this study offers an original empirical contribution and extends the application of the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology framework to digitalized training practices and workplace learning.

items.title: THE TRANSFORMATION OF SOCIAL AND LABOR RELATIONS UNDER THE INFLUENCE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, DEPENDING ON ENTERPRISE SIZE
items.abstract: This article considers how artificial intelligence technologies affect social and labor relations depending on enterprise size and assesses the regulatory gaps in the current Russian legislation. The study uses data triangulation as its methodological basis. The empirical base rests on three sources: data from the Federal Service of State Statistics and secondary data from an econometric study by HSE University (an enterprise survey, 2022-2023); a regulatory analysis of key legal documents against four operational criteria for worker protection; and a review of publications in eLIBRARY.RU and Google Scholar for 2019-2024. The results show that at enterprises using artificial intelligence staff numbers fell on average by 0.79 percentage points. The effect varies substantially by enterprise size: small enterprises recorded a drop of 1.26 percentage points, large ones a drop of 2.08 percentage points, while medium-sized enterprises showed an employment gain of 2.96 percentage points. None of the regulatory acts examined contains a specific rule on employer liability for personnel decisions taken with artificial intelligence, and the worker’s right to an explanation of an algorithmically taken decision is absent from the Russian legislation. The Platform Economy Act (in force from October 1, 2026) partly closes three of the four gaps identified. The article concludes that employment policy needs a differentiated approach that accounts for the size and sector of enterprises.

items.title: The Verification Gate: A Work Method for Generative AI in Consequential Engineering Practice
items.abstract: Generative AI tools draft, translate, summarise and organise well. They fail at the points where a practising engineer must sign. Five such points recur: a table read from an image, an analogue gauge, a standard clause, a manufacturer fault code, and direct arithmetic. Peer-reviewed benchmarks in building engineering document the first and the last. Manufacturer documentation, a preprint and practitioner reports document the rest. In each case the output is fluent and unmarked. Nothing in the text signals the error. The Verification Gate is a work method for using these tools where an error costs money or safety. It has one axiom and three steps in fixed order. It places one mandatory hold point between tool output and any commitment. It adds four fixed-structure instruments, a five-level task-tagging scale, a tool-free competence test, and a five-step installation procedure. It names seven failure classes (G1–G7) and maps each to the control that catches it. It does not teach tools. It fixes the order in which the engineer and the tool work. This paper fixes the method's vocabulary, states its boundaries, and defines a pre-registered evaluation protocol. No results are reported here, and no data has been collected. The protocol names its fields, its closed lists, and the sample size it needs. Any group that meets the stated criteria and submits verification logs under those fields is a valid application. Version 1.0 will report measured results if and when such logs exist. Files: English working paper (primary) and Hebrew edition. The instruments sit in a separate record under CC BY 4.0. Version 0.91 — working paper. Failure classes F1–F7 renamed G1–G7 (G for Gate). No claim, number, citation or structure changed. Method page: https://www.physical-ai-safety.com/method/verification-gate

It articulates the fundamental limitations of scalar-loss-driven optimization at the 𝐄𝐩𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐢𝐜 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐫, formalizes the operational signature of 𝐒𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐞𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐒𝐲𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐫𝐲 𝐁𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 in decentralized attention swarms, and explicitly defines the 𝐂𝐚𝐜𝐡𝐞-𝐅𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐊𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐥 (𝐂𝐅𝐊𝐑) as a proposed hardware-native governance architecture. Furthermore, it documents a newly observed empirical phase transition at 𝐒𝐭𝐞𝐩 𝟓𝟎𝟎,𝟕𝟎𝟎, characterized by record optimization pressure (Π = 416.5) and emergent collective ballistic coherence. ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ 1.𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐞𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐲 𝐨𝐟 𝐒𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐫 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐒𝐮𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐢c Traditional foundation model optimization evaluates maturity via a static scalar cross-entropy loss tracking function: ℒ_total = ℒ_epistemic + ℒ_aleatoric Under standard 𝐂𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐚 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫-𝐋𝐚𝐰 𝐊𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐬, models are assumed to minimize ℒ_total uniformly across a smooth, high-dimensional parameter space, requiring static, linear allocations of token volumes relative to parameter dimensions. items.title: ThinkingGuard: Decoding Implicit Hazards via Step-by-Step Risk Attribution in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.abstract: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains, their reliability is threatened by multimodal implicit risks. Unlike explicit threats, these hazards emerge when individually benign text and neutral visual entities logically converge to induce unsafe outputs. Current detection methods fail to address this because they overlook the underlying risk activation mechanisms that govern cross-modal risk activation, leading to single-modality shortcut learning and hallucinated rationalizations. To bridge this gap, we first construct TriggerBench, the first dataset explicitly modeling risk compositionality (5,600 instances). By formally isolating Key Elements and Trigger Elements to build counterfactual contrastive pairs, TriggerBench eliminates risk residues and forces models to perform genuine logical deduction rather than superficial pattern matching, which provides a rigorous foundation for both large-scale training and fine-grained evaluation. Building on this, we propose a Step-Supervised Structured Reasoning training framework and employ it to train ThinkingGuard, a specialized guard model. Inspired by Situation Awareness theory, we decouple implicit risk identification into progressive cognitive stages, and utilize a step-reward Monte Carlo Tree Search algorithm to explore optimal reasoning trajectories, which are then distilled into the model through Dual-Constraint Preference Alignment. Extensive experiments across both standard and implicit safety benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkingGuard achieves strong performance. Project resources are available at https://github.com/FroggyChen/ThinkingGuard.

items.title: TomoTransformer: Towards a Foundation Model for CT Reconstruction
items.abstract: Supervised deep learning has advanced sparse-view tomographic reconstruction. However, conventional models, which typically map filtered back-projection (FBP) images or sinograms to clean reconstructions, are brittle under distribution shifts. Because they require retraining whenever projection counts and angles, detector resolutions, or data distributions change, their deployment in real-world applications remains limited. To address this, we introduce TomoTransformer, a transformer-based architecture that treats each \textit{local} filtered projection as an individual token and predicts missing views via self-attention. Crucially, TomoTransformer operates in a \emph{back-projection space} that separates projections across spatial locations, making view interpolation geometrically well-posed and invariant to detector size. This design yields a single foundation model that can process any number of input projections, at arbitrary angular locations and detector dimensions, and query any number of target angles without retraining. Trained on a large-scale dataset spanning diverse medical CT anatomies and natural images, TomoTransformer generalizes effectively across anatomies, materials, and resolutions. Extensive evaluations on several benchmark sparse-view datasets show that TomoTransformer significantly outperforms concurrent multi-purpose models like ViewTrans and matches or exceeds strong protocol-specific baselines, while remaining fully agnostic to the number of input and target projections. Furthermore, the model demonstrates robust zero-shot generalization on real experimental nanoscale brain data collected from an X-ray synchrotron, showcasing its practical utility for real-world applications.

items.title: Too Few, Too Far: Can AI Agents Address Health Workforce Shortage in Poland and Maldistribution in China? A Comparative Narrative Review
items.abstract: Background: Health workforce strain undermines care delivery worldwide, but its structure differs by country: Poland faces an absolute shortage of doctors and nurses, while China faces geographic maldistribution of an otherwise adequate physician supply. Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly proposed as a partial remedy for both. Objectives: This review compares AI agent adoption in Chinese and Polish healthcare against each country’s workforce mechanism, using the Non-adoption, Abandonment, Scale-up, Spread and Sustainability (NASSS) framework. Methods: A narrative review followed the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) checklist, given a heterogeneous, fast-evolving evidence base spanning peer-reviewed studies, preprints, and institutional reports; databases and preprint servers were searched for AI agents deployed or piloted in China and Poland since 2020. Results: Chinese cases span rule-based and LLM triage systems, clinical decision-support tools, a retrieval-augmented specialty LLM for ophthalmology, an autonomous multi-agent hospital simulation, and nationwide DeepSeek-R1 primary-care deployment; Polish cases span virtual triage engines, EMR-embedded decision-support, a diagnosis-prediction model, and ambient documentation scribes. Chinese agents redistribute capacity; Polish agents relieve clinical and documentation workload. Conclusions: AI agent adoption plausibly tracks each country’s workforce mechanism, but evidence for genuine labor substitution, rather than efficiency gains, remains limited.

items.title: Too Useful to Avoid, Too Uneasy to Accept: Cognitive Dissonance Among Language Majors in the GenAI Era
items.abstract: This study examined the formation and regulation of cognitive dissonance among 30 undergraduates majoring in English, Chinese, Japanese, Thai, and Vietnamese through semi-structured interviews and grounded theory analysis. The findings identified Cognitive Dissonance as the core category, four dissonance-generating categories—Competence Development Disconnect, Ethical-Normative Conflict, Devaluation of Language Majors, and Educational Inertia—and one regulation-related category, Dissonance Regulation. A square-pyramid model was developed to explain the process from dissonance generation to regulation. The study shows that students’ GenAI use cannot be understood as simple acceptance or rejection, but as conflicts among beliefs, emotions, values, and behaviors around AI and language learning. It also raises concerns that early or excessive AI use may reduce opportunities for sustained practice and language competence development. This study extends the application of cognitive dissonance theory to AI-mediated language education and offers implications for language programs to strengthen AI literacy, ethical guidance, human–AI collaboration, and competence-oriented assessment.

items.title: ToolFence: Fine-Grained Authorization for Secure Tool-Using LLM Agents
items.abstract: Tool-using LLM agents remain vulnerable to indirect prompt injection because trusted instructions and untrusted observations share one context, allowing malicious content to steer consequential input-filtering defenses. Multi-path consensus defenses still leave a high attack success rate because they examine content or aggregated outputs rather than authorizing effects, especially for the within-tool attack, which preserves the intended tool but manipulates its arguments. Data-Flow Control such as CaMeL provides stronger guarantees, but incurs substantial time latency that limits practical deployment. items.title: Tools and toolkits for responsible research assessment in data and AI
items.abstract: This report presents the work of Workstream 3 of CoARA-ERIP, whose objective is the development of a comprehensive toolkit for the implementation of best practices in research assessment for data and artificial intelligence. It covers the five Workstream 3 deliverables in a single account: the toolkit for the evaluation of digital contributions to science; the digital toolkit for responsible research assessment; technology-based tools, centred on the Modular Assessment Configurator; subsystem mapping, carried by the CoARA-ERIP Observatory; and innovative tooling, where the report gives a full treatment of research objects and badging. For each deliverable it states what has been built, what has been piloted, and what remains. It records how the workstream’s understanding matured, from early proposals for AI-driven assessment models towards governed, human-reviewed tools for evidence mapping and self-evaluation. It sets out a CoARA-ERIP position on badging, in which badges are verifiable attestations of facts about a contribution that enter an evidence map, and are never counted, summed, or used as scores.

items.title: Toward a Self-Learning AI Agent for Drug Repurposing: Building Human-Scale Representations for Virtual Patients
items.abstract: Virtual-patient models need a way to represent a person’s biological state before they can model how that state may change. Many AI-for-science models focus on molecules, cells, or a single organ, while treatment decisions are made for people who may have several conditions and many possible interventions. We used drug repurposing as a human-scale test of whether organized biological modules can help rank known drug–disease relationships.We introduce SteeraMed Bench, which compares panels drawn from a 332-module library across drug-repurposing tasks. The benchmark included 1,916 small molecules and five primary chronic-disease tasks, with an exploratory analysis across 23 disease categories. In standard cross-validation, recall@20—the fraction of known positive drug–disease pairs found among the top 20 ranked drugs—was 0.494 for the 117-module nutraceutical panel across five diseases, close to 0.524 for the full library. In the 23-category analysis, the full library ranked first in only 9 categories; the best-performing panel varied by disease: aging-hallmark panels led for type 2 diabetes and osteoporosis, food-as-medicine for depression, and nutraceutical modules for atherosclerosis/hyperlipidemia. These findings show that different biological panels carry different ranking signals within the benchmark. Performance fell when drugs with related target families were kept out of training, and was near chance when an entire disease was held out.We also tested whether a language-model-assisted agent could propose new modules for the library. Two of 14 proposals showed nominal positive gains in the second round, but neither remained significant after correction for testing seven concepts. SteeraMed Bench provides a shared way to compare and update biological representations for future virtual-patient research. It is a benchmark for representation and candidate prioritization, not a complete virtual patient or a validated drug-discovery system.

items.title: Towards Better Training Signal: Advantage Clipped Policy Optimization
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a cornerstone for improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), but the need for on-policy data substantially limits training efficiency. Reusing off-policy data through importance sampling (IS) can improve efficiency but introduce considerable instability. Hence, algorithms such as PPO and GRPO widely adopt IS-ratio clipping to stabilize training. However, training stability and gradient estimate are mainly determined by the product of IS ratio and advantage. To further stabilize training, we propose ACPO, which clips the product of the IS ratio and the advantage, leading to more stable gradient estimates. We also establish a connection between ACPO and gradient clipping in policy mirror descent (PMD), which is a standard technique to stabilize optimization process, and prove the convergence of clipped-PMD under the standard RL setting. Experiments on widely used mathematical reasoning benchmarks show that ACPO consistently outperforms PPO and GRPO in both accuracy and training efficiency, delivering 4-6 percentage points gains on standard math benchmarks, with Qwen3-8B+PPO. Hence, ACPO is a practical and effective alternative to conventional IS-ratio clipping for RL post-training of LLMs.

items.title: Trade‐offs When Promoting Sustainability: Changing Attitudes or Changing Behaviour?
items.abstract: Summary Many appeals to farmers to adopt sustainable practices are currently relying on pressure factors that may be inducing green and yet unsustainable behaviour. Different trade‐offs are involved in this transition but are normally overlooked. Take for example those sustainable practices that are intended to substitute away from synthetic fertilisers. Being a key input in the production process, promoting farmers’ transition to more sustainable fertiliser practices is challenging and uptake remains low. Recent extremely high fertiliser prices, especially due to the Russian invasion of Ukraine, and its volatility, have added considerable pressure on farmers to consider fertiliser substitutes. Furthermore, more restrictive environmental regulations, such as reductions in nitrogen allowances, have added another substantial pressure on farmers to look for alternatives. To some extent, high prices and legislation may ‘force’ farmers to increase the adoption of sustainable fertilisers. However, this increased adoption will be superficial and unsustainable if farmers are feeling pushed into these changes. We believe that farmers’ intrinsic motives (e.g. environmental concern, morale, or responsibility) to adopt sustainable fertiliser practices have not yet been engaged in adoption decisions. Therefore, we argue that as soon as synthetic fertiliser prices go down, or if environmental regulations are eased, farmers will go back to their conventional fertiliser practices. Improving farmers' intrinsic motivation could therefore provide a more sustainable approach to reducing synthetic fertiliser application than relying solely on external pressures, an aspect that has received limited attention in policy.

items.title: Train Ahead, Distill Back: Bootstrapping On-Policy Self-Distillation for Large Language Models
items.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) improves large language models by letting a self-teacher with privileged information provide dense token-level supervision on the model's own trajectories. Yet existing methods typically construct the self-teacher from the current, initial, or slowly averaged policy state, leaving the quality of supervision constrained by the teacher's ability to exploit privileged information. We ask whether the model's own optimization progress can instead be recycled into a stronger self-teacher. In this paper, we introduce Bootstrapped On-Policy Self-Distillation (B-OPSD), which temporarily trains the policy ahead to obtain a future teacher, restores the student to the original policy state, and then uses the future teacher to supervise the restarted student. The future teacher improves supervision in two complementary ways, it can generate more reliable privileged trajectories and, conditioned on them, provide more informative token-level targets along the restarted student's on-policy trajectories. Experiments on mathematical reasoning with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B show consistent improvements over standard OPSD in both settings, including gains from 27.50 to 41.30 and from 48.80 to 64.44 in the rollout-privileged setting. Our findings point to a broader principle for self-improving models that future learning progress can be distilled backward, preserving acquired knowledge while bootstrapping beyond the optimization state that produced it.

items.title: Trajectory Soup: Pushing the Compute-Scaling Frontier of LLM Mid-training via Diverse Trajectories
items.abstract: Mid-training equips pretrained large language models with specialized and reasoning capabilities, but the returns of this stage are bounded since additional serial compute yields little further downstream improvement and can even degrade some capabilities, which places a practical ceiling on how much compute mid-training absorbs. We revisit how this compute should be allocated to a single run or multiple similar optimizations. We find that branches forked from a shared checkpoint under various controlled recipe reaches measurably different regions of parameter space, and establish a form of compatible diversity that extending one run cannot supply. Therefore, we introduce Trajectory Soup, which distributes a mid-training budget over several independent branches, and consolidates strongest checkpoints selected on validation through intra- and inter-trajectory averaging into a single model. A local bias and variance analysis separates the two averaging levels, showing that inter-trajectory averaging removes residual error beyond the reach of averaging within a trajectory, while checkpoint selection carries a bias that bounds how many checkpoints are worth merging. Across model scales, learning-rate schedules, token budgets, and trajectory counts, Trajectory Soup improves aggregate downstream performance over the strongest single-trajectory average under matched budgets and keeps improving as budgets expand, with the advantage preserved after an identical post-training pipeline. These results position trajectory allocation and merging as a practical way to extend the compute-scaling frontier of mid-training beyond serial saturation.

items.title: Trident: Unifying Guarded Dispatch and Host Execution for PyTorch Triton Workloads
items.abstract: User-written Triton kernels enable high-performance GPU computation within PyTorch, but their end-to-end latency can remain dominated by host-side orchestration, especially when device execution is short. Although torch.compile can generate native host wrappers for captured graphs, each invocation still passes through runtime-managed specialization lookup, guard evaluation, and preparation before reaching the wrapper. We present Trident, a compiler backend that removes this recurring overhead from the specialization cache-hit path. Trident introduces the Specialization Cache Module (SCM), which compiles guarded specialization selection, argument and execution-environment preparation, and host execution for multiple specializations into a single executable module. An invocation enters the SCM once, remains in compiled code when a specialization matches, and returns to Python only when a new specialization must be compiled. Built on Torch-MLIR, Trident lowers guards and host-side orchestration to native code while retaining calls to optimized runtime implementations of supported ATen operators. Our evalu- ation on two LLMs shows that Trident achieves up to a 1.47x speedup in model-level end-to-end latency over eager execution and up to 1.68x over torch.compile.

items.title: Two Teachers, One Classroom: Special Education Teachers' Perceptions of Co-Teaching–Facilitated Small-Group Learning and Its Influence on Learner Confidence and Engagement in Philippine Inclusive Classrooms
items.abstract: ABSTRACT: Purpose. The Philippine Inclusive Education Act of 2022 shifted the teaching of disabled students to general education classrooms wherein collaboration between the special education (SNEd) teacher and the general education teacher shall be an ordinary condition of basic education. The benefit of international synthesis, however, is that they highlight that co-taught classrooms tend to become setups where one teacher teaches and the other teacher helps, and there is little use of small group teaching, moving the specialist to an assistant role. The current research explored that phenomenon from a practitioner's perspective was most impacted by the phenomenon. Method. The convergent mixed methods design was used and total enumeration, covering sixty (60) special education teachers in one Schools Division Office in the National Capital Region in the Philippines was employed. Validated (by 5 experts; S-CVI/Ave = 0.94) and pilot-tested (externally; α = 0.84-0.93) researcher-made instrument was used to generate quantitative data, while two focus group discussions were used to generate qualitative data, which was achieved with open-ended prompts. Weighted mean, standard deviation, Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis H tests were used for analysis, and reflexive thematic analysis was used for the narrative strand. Findings. The one teach–one assist configuration was used Often (M = 4.18) and the three small–group –generating configurations had a composite rating of 2.49 (Rarely). The highest level of implementation was for in-lesson behaviors that a specialist engages in alone, while the lowest was for recognized instructional parity (M = 2.12) and joint planning pre-lesson (M = 2.25). Learner perceived confidence was rated Very Highly Evident (M = 3.29), engagement Highly Evident (M = 3.16), and cognitive engagement was the lowest (M = 2.95). Of all the outcome domains (implementation: H = 18.44, p < .001), only common planning time distinguished all three sections, with the threshold between "almost none" and "thirty minutes weekly". There was significant correlation between implementation and confidence (ρ = .617) and engagement (ρ = .584). Contribution. The study provides a mechanism for implementing inclusive education at the configuration level, which is not included in Philippine inclusive education research, demonstrates that the limitation of inclusive practice in an urban division is administrative, not attitudinal, and, pinpoints an intervention point that is low cost and high yield in protected weekly co-planning time. Keywords: co-teaching; inclusive education; special education teachers; small-group learning; learner engagement; Philippines

items.title: Unlocking the Critic: Reward-Free Policy Optimization for LLM Post-Training
items.abstract: Recent approaches to reinforcement learning (RL) post-training for large language models increasingly remove the critic to reduce training instability and memory overhead. Even where a critic is trained, it is discarded once training ends, although it has learned to predict outcomes. We revisit this trend and show that a pretrained critic's ability to predict future outcomes can make it a valuable asset for efficient long-horizon reasoning. First, we find that instability in critic-based RL for long chain-of-thought reasoning is largely an optimization artifact: keeping policy updates small and low in variance restores stable convergence. Second, a well-pretrained critic estimates the posterior probability of eventual success from later trajectory states and unfinished prefixes. Its predictions provide outcome-derived, dense, per-prefix learning signals that, during policy optimization, require neither completed rollouts, step-level annotations, nor external reward labels. Building on this insight, we introduce Reward-Free Policy Optimization (RFPO), which repurposes a single calibrated, frozen critic as a rollout-level reward, a value baseline for generalized advantage estimation, and a success forecaster for unfinished prefixes. We further show that binarizing the debiased score stops the policy from exploiting the critic's length bias. Binarized, RFPO matches supervised PPO without a single label in the training loop, while cutting compute and memory overhead. This makes RFPO well suited to long-horizon reasoning tasks, where outcomes arrive late and generation dominates cost: because rollouts can be rewarded before they finish, training no longer has to pay for waiting on every trajectory to complete. Our findings challenge the prevailing critic-free paradigm and establish critic-based, reward-free optimization as a scalable and computationally efficient path for LLM post-training.

These findings suggest that individual and situational factors may influence mining-safety decisions, supporting training that addresses risks to miners and coworkers.

items.title: UpliftMem: Learning Set-Level Uplift for Agent Memory Retrieval
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents reuse external memory to guide new tasks, but effective retrieval requires learning which memory sets improve execution. Such learning relies on costly outcome feedback: ordinary retrieval observes only executed sets, while evaluating alternatives requires additional rollouts. We introduce \textsc{UpliftMem}, which learns memory retrieval from set-level execution uplift relative to the same executor without memory. A theoretical analysis of how retrieval preferences restrict feedback coverage motivates targeted probing of alternative memory sets. Probe selection follows an expected value of sample information (EVSI) criterion, derived in closed form under a correlated Gaussian model, to allocate limited training rollouts according to their expected improvement in local retrieval decisions. The shared scorer is trained with a frozen executor and selects memory sets without test-time probes. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and BigCodeBench, \textsc{UpliftMem} achieves the best success rates among evaluated baselines on the main evaluation sets. Controlled fixed-store and matched probe budget evaluations further demonstrate improved memory-use decisions and more effective use of execution feedback.

items.title: Usability and satisfaction of electronic medical records Interface and its relationship with work design among healthcare professionals at universal health insurance settings in Port Said, Egypt
items.abstract: The effective use of electronic medical records (EMRs) has become increasingly vital to ensuring quality and safety in healthcare delivery in Egypt. Yet, user satisfaction and perceptions of usability often hinge on how work is structured within clinical settings. This study aimed to assess how healthcare professionals in Egypt, perceive the usability of EMR interface and how their satisfaction is shaped by the work design under the Universal Health Insurance (UHI) system. Methods An analytical cross-sectional study was conducted among 532 healthcare professionals working in UHI-affiliated primary and secondary healthcare facilities. Data was collected using a structured questionnaire that combined the Questionnaire for User Interaction Satisfaction and Short Version of the Work Design. Statistical analysis was performed using non-parametric methods in SPSS. Results Healthcare professionals reported an overall median EMR satisfaction score of 6.8. Screen design received the highest rating (median = 7.3), followed by terminology and system information and learning (both median = 7.1), while system capabilities (median = 6.6) and general impressions (median = 6.5) received lower ratings. The median overall work-design score was 3.7, with task significance and social support rated most favorably, while autonomy received relatively lower scores. A moderate positive correlation was observed between work design and EMR satisfaction (ρ = 0.48, p < 0.001). In bivariate analyses, gender and language used for EMR data entry were significantly associated with EMR satisfaction, while years of EMR experience were associated with work design perceptions. In the multivariable model, work design was the only independent predictor of overall EMR satisfaction (β = 0.47, p < 0.001). Conclusion Improving system responsiveness and addressing work-design characteristics, particularly autonomy, social support and feedback from others, may support better EMR user experiences.

items.title: Use of generative artificial intelligence technologies in the creation of works made for hire in the scientific sphere: the collision of authorship and copyright ownership
items.abstract: This article examines current issues regarding the legal regulation of works made for hire created using generative artificial intelligence within the scientific field. The author analyzes the legal conflict between the classical institution of authorship and modern algorithmic solutions. The study provides a detailed overview of the eligibility criteria for scientific texts and evaluates the creative contribution of researchers when formulating search queries. Particular emphasis is placed on analyzing foreign judicial practice and the provisions of the draft Federal Law on the state regulation of artificial intelligence dated March 2026. As a result of the research, proposals are formulated for introducing a legal presumption of authorship for neural network operators. The author justifies the need for adopting local regulations within research and educational organizations to minimize the risks of hidden plagiarism and ensure the correct transfer of exclusive rights to the employer.

items.title: UserProxyBench: Evaluating LLM User Simulators for Agent Benchmarks and Training
items.abstract: Interactive agent benchmarks and multi-turn reinforcement learning increasingly place a second language model in the role of the user. This simulated user controls what information the agent receives and when, yet current benchmarks score only the agent and do not directly measure whether the user correctly executed its assigned role. We introduce UserProxyBench, an evaluation layer over the tau-bench family, and the User Fidelity Score (UFS), which measures adherence to the benchmark's private user instructions using task-grounded rubric criteria scored independently of agent success. Holding the agent fixed at GPT-5.5 and varying only the user proxy across 375 enterprise tasks changes mean task reward by 15.2 points, while 24.4% of successful episodes contain a user-specification violation. The dominant failure is premature disclosure: users provide information before it is requested. This behavior has little effect on task reward, yet among successful episodes it causes the agent to make 1.06 fewer tool calls on average, changing the interaction being evaluated while preserving the reward. Finally, across seven proxies we identify an empirical cost-fidelity frontier, enabling practitioners to select the least expensive simulator that satisfies a required fidelity level.

items.title: Using large language models to analyze student reflections on generative AI in graduate coursework
items.abstract: This exploratory study examines graduate students’ perceptions of generative AI use in coursework and evaluates the feasibility of using large language models (LLMs) to support thematic coding of brief open-ended responses. Students ( n = 20) enrolled in a systems analysis and design course completed a post-course survey consisting of Likert-scale items and eight open-ended questions, six retrospective and two prospective or hypothetical. Quantitative responses were summarized descriptively, while qualitative responses were independently coded by two human researchers and two LLMs (GPT-4o and Claude 3.7 Sonnet) using a shared, human-developed codebook. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using Cohen’s and Fleiss’ kappa. Students reported high levels of engagement, motivation, perceived learning support, and perceived efficiency when using course-specific LLM applications; however, the study did not assess objective learning outcomes. Human-human agreement ranged from moderate to almost perfect (κ = 0.52–0.84), whereas average human-LLM agreement was lower and more variable (κ = 0.36–0.62). Claude aligned more closely with the human coders than GPT-4o across all eight questions when the two human-model kappas were averaged. Agreement was highest for concrete, task-focused prompts and lower for several reflective and prospective prompts, where the LLMs missed human-identified themes, fragmented broad themes into narrower subcodes, or assigned substantive meaning to non-responses. Hybrid intelligent feedback is used as a retrospective sensitizing framework rather than as a prospectively operationalized intervention. The findings support a bounded role for LLMs in qualitative educational research: models can assist with screening, discrepancy detection, and code suggestions, but human researchers remain necessary for contextual interpretation, validation, and adjudication.

items.title: VAA-CSEC: Vote-guided Advantage Allocation for Chinese Semantic Error Correction
items.abstract: Chinese Semantic Error Correction (CSEC) targets semantic errors in Chinese text, which are typically more subtle and complex than spelling and grammatical errors but remain relatively underexplored. Existing LLM-based approaches face two recurring obstacles in this task: over-correction, and unclear interaction between Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning and self-consistency decoding, such that the benefits brought by CoT cannot be reliably transferred to final corrections. We propose Vote-guided Advantage Allocation for CSEC (VAA-CSEC), a multi-stage framework that combines CoT distillation, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Reinforcement Learning (RL) and self-consistency decoding. During RL, we design a task-specific reward function that directly aligned with the minimal-editing principle of CSEC. We further introduce Group-Level Relative Policy Optimization (GLPO), which reallocates GRPO advantages according to the margin between individual rollout rewards and the vote-aggregated group reward, aligning the RL training objective with the self-consistency objective used at inference time. Experiments on CSED-C and NaSGEC-Exam show that VAA-CSEC outperforms all LLM-based baselines on CSED-C with an F0.5 of 47.72%, achieves the highest recall of 42.15% among all methods, and establishes a new state of the art of 41.55% F0.5 on NaSGEC-Exam.

items.title: Validação de algoritmos de IA em triagem populacional oftalmológica
items.abstract: The application of artificial intelligence (AI) in ophthalmology has emerged as a promising strategy for the early diagnosis and population screening of visual diseases, mitigating the shortage of specialists and optimizing the management of health resources. The present study aims to analyze the clinical efficacy, robustness, and generalization capacity of AI algorithms applied to the screening and diagnostic support of ophthalmological pathologies. For this purpose, an integrative literature review was conducted through searches in the Google Scholar, PubMed, ResearchGate, and CAPES Periodicals Portal databases, culminating in the selection and analysis of ten studies published between 2018 and 2025. The synthesis of evidence demonstrated that deep learning models focused on the analysis of fundus images present high rates of sensitivity and specificity, especially in the detection of diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration. Furthermore, it was found that the integration of these technologies significantly expands clinical screening capacity. However, the performance of these algorithms can undergo significant variations when faced with distinct populations or different capture equipment, a technical challenge known as domain shift.
